summary: Mexico shed more than 500,000 industrial jobs in June, with services also posting sharp losses despite the World Cup, deepening signs of a weakening labor market. On the trade front, the United States reopened its border to Mexican cattle imports after a year-long ban meant to curb beef prices, while Mexican and US officials wrapped a third round of talks on the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review, agreeing to meet again in Washington in September. Separately, Mexico's central bank is pushing simplified Level 2 Bis accounts to boost digital payments among small businesses.

items.headline: United States reopens border to Mexican cattle imports after year-long ban
items.context: The US had blocked Mexican cattle for more than a year to contain rising beef prices for American consumers. The reopening is meant to ease pressure on meat costs while keeping monitoring in place.

items.headline: Third round of trade agreement review ends with plans for September meeting
items.context: Mexican and US officials completed a third round of technical talks on the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement and agreed to reconvene in Washington in September, part of the pact's first mandated joint review.
items.drivers: Talks focused on steel, aluminum and derivative products, regional value chains, and reducing reliance on Asian imports, led by Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard and US trade office Jamieson Greer.
items.next: The two governments will hold a fourth round of talks in the first half of September to continue the joint review.
